takeaways: Files are the primary abstraction for persistent data and are identified by names and attributes.
Directories form a hierarchical namespace that lets users organize files logically.
Mounting connects an external file system to the existing directory tree, enabling file sharing across devices.
Different block‑allocation strategies trade off space efficiency, access speed, and fragmentation.
Free‑space management (bitmap or free list) lets the OS locate unused blocks quickly.
Polling, interrupts and DMA are hardware mechanisms that affect CPU utilisation during I/O.
Device drivers, buffering and caching form the software stack that hides device details and improves performance.
Disk geometry (cylinders, tracks, sectors) and scheduling algorithms reduce mechanical seek time.
bank_note: Syllabi stress clear definitions, step‑by‑step explanations and comparison of design choices for long‑answer questions on file‑system concepts and I/O management.

bank.q: Define a file. List its main attributes and describe the two basic access methods.
outline: Attributes such as name, size, type, timestamps, permissions

bank.q: Draw a three‑level directory tree containing at least five files. Explain how the OS resolves an absolute pathname.
outline: Tree diagram with root, sub‑directory, leaf files
Step‑by‑step pathname lookup from root to leaf
Role of directory entries and inode numbers

bank.q: A USB flash drive is inserted. Describe the sequence of operations the OS performs to mount the file system and make its files available to the user.
Compare contiguous, linked and indexed allocation. For each method discuss space utilisation, access time and fragmentation.
A disk has 1024 blocks. After allocating blocks 5‑10 and 200‑205, show the bitmap representation of the first 210 blocks and explain how the OS would locate the next free block.
outline: Bitmap with 0 for free, 1 for used

bank.q: Explain polling, interrupts and DMA. Evaluate their impact on CPU utilisation and I/O latency for a high‑throughput network card.
Detail the steps performed by a device driver when a user process issues a read() system call that uses DMA for data transfer.
outline: Copy to user buffer if needed

bank.q: Define buffering and caching. Give one example where each improves system performance.
For the request queue 55, 58, 39, 18, 90 and initial head position 50, compute total head movement for FCFS, SSTF, SCAN and C‑SCAN algorithms.
Explain how a Virtual File System (VFS) enables mounting of both ext4 and FAT32 file systems under a common root directory.
outline: Path resolution across different concrete file systems

bank.q: In a multi‑user environment, describe how the OS enforces file sharing permissions using directory entries, inode metadata and optional Access Control Lists.
outline: Owner, group, others bits in inode

bank.q: List the main components of the storage hierarchy from fastest to slowest and explain why the OS uses caching at each level.
outline: Registers, L1/L2 cache, main memory, SSD, HDD, tape
Cache purpose (temporal/spatial locality) at each level

bank.q: A sudden power cut in Chennai shuts down a server. Describe how a journaling file system recovers to a consistent state after power is restored.
